author: Athanasius of Alexandria
occasion: Athanasius offers interpretive notes on select verses of Job, using them to refute Arian claims that the Son is a creature and to explain how created beings, angels, and the devil relate to God's uncontained nature.
argument: Athanasius argues that Scripture's use of 'made' or 'became' for sons does not prove the Son of God is a creature, since the same language is used for natural children. He then explains that created beings, including angels and the devil, are located and changeable, while God alone is unbounded and unchangeable. The devil deceives by disguising himself, but Christ has exposed his illusions. Finally, Athanasius interprets Job's cosmic language about mountains, the shaking of heaven, and the stars as referring to Christ's renewal of the old covenant and the events of his passion.

outline.move: Athanasius refutes the Arian use of 'made him' by showing Scripture applies 'made' and 'became' to natural children, so the Son's being begotten is not denied by such language; he then explains that created beings occupy places while God is unbounded, and that 'standing before the Lord' means being conformed to God's will.
He presents Job's endurance as the mark of courage, and explains how the devil deceives by counterfeiting truth, as he did with Eve and Job's wife.

This section recapitulates themes from sections 1 and 2: the spatial boundedness of created beings and God's unboundedness, the meaning of 'standing before the Lord,' Job's endurance, and the devil's deceptions; it then introduces the interpretation of mountains as the prophets.

He interprets the mountains as the prophets aged by Christ, explains that the Jews did not recognize this aging, and treats the shaking of heaven, the darkened sun, and the named stars as figures of Christ's passion and cosmic signs, including an astronomical discussion of why Job named Pleiades, Hesperus, and Arcturus.

cast.name: Job
cast.who: The righteous sufferer whose endurance and speeches Athanasius interprets.

cast.name: the devil
cast.who: The deceiver who tempts Job and counterfeits God's words; also called the serpent who deceived Eve and Job's wife.

cast.name: Job's wife
cast.who: Deceived by the devil into urging blasphemy against God.

cast.name: Eve
cast.who: The first woman, deceived by the serpent through counterfeit divine words.

cast.name: Hezekiah
cast.who: King cited from Isaiah as using 'make' for begetting children.

cast.name: Moses
cast.who: Lawgiver and prophet, cited for legal language and as one of the 'mountains' Christ ages.

cast.name: the Arians
cast.who: Opponents who claim the Son is a creature based on 'faithful to him who made him.'

cast.name: the apostles
cast.who: Identified as the 'pillars' shaken at the time of Christ's passion, scandalized according to Christ's prediction.

cast.name: the Jews
cast.who: Those who did not recognize that the old covenant was being aged and renewed.

voices.speaker: Scripture (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Quoted phrases from Job, Psalms, Isaiah, Hebrews, and the Gospels, often introduced by 'it says' or embedded without introduction.

voices.speaker: God/the Lord (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as speaking to the devil: 'And God said to the devil: Where have you come from?' and 'And the Lord said to the devil: Where have you come from?'

voices.speaker: Hezekiah (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as praying in Isaiah: 'From today I will make children.'

voices.speaker: the Spirit (quoted)
voices.how_marked: Introduced as commanding in the psalm: 'Be strong, and let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord.'

key_terms.sense: A thing made or created, as opposed to a begotten son.
That which is begotten, a natural offspring.
Not contained or bounded by place, said only of God.
Endurance under trial, the mark of courage in the saints.
The devil's deceptive appearance or illusion by which he counterfeits truth.
To stand before the Lord, explained as being conformed to his will, not being in a place.
Created things, which are changeable and located in places.
Mountains, interpreted as the prophets, especially Moses and those after him.
Making old, used of Christ aging the old covenant and its written letter.
The new covenant brought by Christ, contrasted with the old letter.
Pillars of the earth, interpreted as the apostles shaken at the passion.

scripture: Athanasius cites the Septuagint, using Greek book names and LXX Psalm numbering. Modern citations should use standard English Bible book names and, where applicable, note LXX Psalm numbering in parentheses if it differs from the Hebrew.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is not established from the source.
The original addressee or occasion of the notes is not stated in the source.
The precise identity of the 'some' who call Arcturus the 'bear-keeper' is not specified.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the devil: 'also called the serpent who deceived Eve and Job's wife'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: ὁ τῆς κακίας εὑρετής, ὁ δόλιος, ὁ πειράζων, ὁ μαχόμενος
_unresolved_facts.fix: The devil is called 'the inventor of evil' (ὁ τῆς κακίας εὑρετής), 'the deceitful one' (ὁ δόλιος), 'the tempter' (ὁ πειράζων), and 'the one fighting' (ὁ μαχόμενος). The serpent (ὄφις) is mentioned as the one who deceived Eve and Job's wife, but the text does not explicitly identify the devil as the serpent; it says Job's wife was 'deceived by the serpent' (ἐξαπατηθεῖσαν ὑπὸ τοῦ ὄφεως) and Eve was deceived the same way.

_unresolved_facts.claim: the apostles: 'Identified as the 'pillars' shaken at the time of Christ's passion, scandalized according to Christ's prediction.'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: οἱ δὲ στύλοι αὐτῆς σαλεύοντες, δηλονότι οἱ ἀπόστολοι ἐν τῷ καιρῷ τοῦ πάθους ἐσαλεύθησαν Πάντες ὑμεῖς, φησὶ, σκανδαλισθήσεσθε ἐν ἐμοὶ ἐν τῇ νυκτὶ ταύτῃ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The apostles are identified as 'the pillars' (οἱ στύλοι) that were shaken (ἐσαλεύθησαν), but the quotation 'All of you will be scandalized in me this night' is attributed to Christ with 'φησὶ' (he says), not as a direct quotation formula. The brief should note the apostles were shaken/scandalized, not that they are 'scandalized according to Christ's prediction' as a separate claim.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Section 4: 'including an astronomical discussion of why Job named Pleiades, Hesperus, and Arcturus'
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ταῦτα ὑπὲρ ἐμέ ἐστι τὰ μαθήματα. Πολλῶν γὰρ ὄντων τῶν ἀστέρων Πλειάδων, πλανητῶν καὶ ἀπλάνων παραλεγομένων ὑπὸ τῶν μὴ εἰδότων ὡς αὐτοὶ νομίζουσιν (ἔστι καὶ Ἕσπερος, ἐστι καὶ Φαέτων, καὶ Φαίνων, καὶ Στίλβων καὶ Φωσφόρος) τί δήποτε οὖν ὁ Ἰὼβ ἐν Πνεύματι φθεγγόμενος ἀπὸ τοσούτων ἀστέρων τῶν ἐν τῷ ἀπλάνει τὴν Πλείαδα μόνην ὠνόμασε; καὶ ἀπὸ τοσούτων πλανητῶν λεγομένων Ἕσπερον μόνον εἴρηκε; καὶ ἄλλον ἕνα τὸν Ἀρκτοῦρον τὸν ἐν τῷ ἀρκτοῦν ὄντα, τὸν λεγόμενον ὑπό τινων ἀρκτοφύλακα;
_unresolved_facts.fix: The discussion is not 'astronomical' in a technical sense but a question about why Job named only these three stars/constellations out of many. Athanasius poses this as a question ('why ever did Job...name only the Pleiades?') without providing an answer in the extant text. The brief should say 'raising a question about why Job named only Pleiades, Hesperus, and Arcturus among the many stars' rather than 'an astronomical discussion of why.'

_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Καὶ εἶπεν ὁ Θεὸς τῷ διαβόλῳ· Πόθεν παραγέγονας; Ἀθανασίου.
_unresolved_facts.fix: In section 1, the quotation 'And God said to the devil: Where have you come from?' is followed by 'Ἀθανασίου' (of Athanasius), which appears to be a section marker or attribution, not part of the quotation. The brief correctly notes this appears in section 1, but should verify this is a quotation formula rather than a marginal note. The section 3 occurrence is clear.
